newsitem.title: USA: Canadian natural gas price rally seen not over yet.
newsitem.headline: Canadian natural gas price rally seen not over yet.

text.p: Canadian domestic and export natural gas prices, which have soared to the highest levels of the year, still have some more upside potential, some market sources said Friday.
"We should be close to the top, but the fact remains that there is still a shortage in supply," said one U.S. trader.
In early Friday trading, prices at the AECO storage hub in southeastern Alberta remained strong in the C$1.55-1.57 per gigajoule (GJ) range, up more than 30 cents from October 1.
Fueling the rally is cold weather in the Northwest and diminishing storage supplies, industry sources said.
Traders estimated that about 500-700 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas has been withdrawn from storage in Alberta over the last 10 days.
Draining supply further is the dwindling gas in western U.S. storage.

According to the American Gas Association, gas in storage in the western states dropped two billion cubic feet (bcf) to 339 bcf, or 70 percent of capacity, in the week ending October 25. This is compared to 424 bcf in storage a year ago.
"There's more potential to move up than down. I think the bottom (of the AECO market) is right around the C$1.55 per GJ level," said one Calgary-based trader.
Temperatures are currently seasonable in western Canada, but forecasts are calling for a return to colder weather by next week.

The western Canadian export market has shown the sharpest move in prices. Swing prices at Sumas, Wash., have surged as high as $2.50 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), traders said, up an average of $1.30, or 155 percent from October 1.
"There's more upside potential if it gets cold," said one export trader, adding the $3 level was possible.
"We're not going to reach $1.10 again anytime soon," he added.
However, the full return of Northwest Pipeline's Chehalis compressor station in Washington Monday could temper another significant price rally at Sumas in the near-term, traders speculated.
The partial outage, which began on October 1 and affected about 150-190 mmcfd of gas, was extended by three days to November 3.

In eastern Canada, cold weather also pushed gas prices much higher at the Niagara export point. The swing market was talked in the $3.12-3.18 per mmBtu area, up about $1 from October 1, while deals were done for the entire month in the $3.25 area, traders said.
